Runtime failure detection for generative robot policies

Six detectors, ranked by how little each must be told before it can warn you.

Weekly update, 29 September 2026 · compiled 18 September

Detector comparison

Every paper here answers the same question: the policy is running, when should you stop trusting it? They split on what they read the answer off, and the split is sharper than the accuracy numbers suggest. Three descend from SAFE's probe on the hidden state, three from resampling the policy's own actions, and only two of the six can work having never been shown a failure.

Ranks come from four questions asked of every detector:

  • C1 Does it score the forward pass the policy already ran, with no resampling and no second model?
  • C2 Does it work without reaching inside the policy for weights or activations?
  • C3 Does it work on any policy architecture, rather than one action-head family?
  • C4 Does it hold up off its own bench, on unseen tasks, a second policy family, and a real robot?

The tier is what you must hand the detector before it can run. It is the one thing in this set that forms a strict ladder, each rung containing the one above it, and it is the constraint the papers themselves argue about.

  • Tier 1, calibrate only Fits nothing. A handful of successful rollouts set a threshold, and that is the whole of its preparation.
  • Tier 2, fit on successes Trains a model, but never sees a failure.
  • Tier 3, fit on both Needs failed rollouts alongside successful ones, labelled at the level of the whole trajectory.
  • Tier 4, fit on marked onsets Needs a human to watch each failure and mark the step it began.

C1 to C4 describe an entry; they do not order it. They cut across the tier rather than stacking, which is the finding rather than a defect in the scoring: the detector that needs least is also the narrowest, and the one scoring four ticks needs failures to get them. Within a tier the order comes from head-to-head results, wherever one paper evaluated another on its own setup, which is what puts TDQC above SAFE on three fewer ticks. C4 is where the field is weakest: two of the six were never run on a real robot at all.

Ranking detail · the table, what each ingredient is worth, and what breaks the ties

Each paper uses its own policies, benchmarks and metrics, and only LIBERO is shared by all six. Every number below is read from the paper itself rather than from a summary.

Ties break on head-to-head results wherever one paper evaluated another on its own setup, with one caveat: a re-run baseline drops. SAFE-MLP on OpenVLA+WidowX unseen is 88.42 in its own paper and 83.18 in TDQC's; on π0+LIBERO unseen it is 73.27 in its own paper and 67.7 in FailureSpot's, though that split reserves seven tasks as unseen against SAFE's three. The geometry paper fits SAFE on 16 successful and 16 failed rollouts and FIPER on 32 successful, against FIPER's own 50. No ordering here is a measured gap.

SAFE is the hub of this set. Four of the other five run it as a baseline and name it as the state of the art they are displacing, and two of those four run its released codebase directly, TDQC on its rollouts as well. FIPER is the exception and does not cite it at all, which is why its numbers sit in a different currency from everyone else's here.

What the early warning is actually worth

Five of the six ablate their own contribution. Read as ingredients rather than as systems, they separate cleanly.

PaperIngredientWorthMeasured against
FIPERRequiring an out-of-distribution observation and a dispersed action distribution+14 points of timestep-wise accuracy, 0.65 against 0.51, all of it from the true-negative rate, 0.65 against 0.05the same two scores combined with OR, which flags nearly every rollout
FailureSpotA 15% human timestamp-annotation budget30.7 → 90.5 timestamp AUROC on π0 unseen; of that, active selection over random is 12.2 and the weak-supervision pretrain over plain trajectory labels is 10.4its own action-derived weak supervision, run alone
ActProbeComparing consecutive chunks where they natively overlap72.1 against 68.4 on unseen tasks, with plain squared error beating both STAC's maximum mean discrepancy and FIPER's binned entropyeliciting the same disagreement by resampling K chunks
accelTruncating the read to the first half of the denoise0.541 → 0.792 Spearman against the resampling reference on π0.5+LIBEROthe full path, whose last Euler steps carry the most discretisation noise
TDQCA temporal-difference target in place of cross-entropyBrier improves in every benchmark, but ROC-AUC moves +5.9, +0.4 and −3.9 depending on where it is dropped inthe same head trained with binary cross-entropy

The last row is the one worth dwelling on. Better-calibrated probabilities and better-ranked rollouts are related, TDQC measures the correlation at ρ = −0.686, but they are not the same objective, and only one of them is what a monitor is scored on.

Conformal prediction is the inherited part, and two of the six threw it out

Four papers calibrate with the same functional conformal band, citing Diquigiovanni et al. and, after SAFE, each other. Only FIPER proves anything about the predictor it actually deploys: bounding each leg does not bound their conjunction, since the two scores are not independent. The other two replaced the band outright, the geometry paper with a CUSUM height after arguing a time-indexed threshold degenerates on long horizons, ActProbe with a single split-conformal cutoff it calls simpler to deploy. Two independent rejections of the same imported machinery, by the two papers that also report the most stable numbers, is the strongest signal here that the conformal layer is carried rather than load-bearing.

Why each ranks where it does

The mechanism behind each entry is in its node card; what follows is only the comparison.

  • accel (#1) The only entry that fits nothing at all: fifty successful rollouts set a threshold and the preparation ends there. It is also the only detector in its own table that never collapses, where STAC drops to 0.06 on π0.5+RoboCasa. Its rank is bought narrow, though: flow-matching heads only, never a real robot, and silent when the model is confidently wrong.
  • FIPER (#2) Fits a model, but only on successes, which is the whole of its argument: failures cannot be manufactured safely, so a detector that needs them cannot be prepared. It is the only guarantee in the set that covers what it actually deploys. It is also the one entry that fails C1, resampling 32 chunks per decision step, and it was never run on a large vision-language-action model.
  • ActProbe (#3) The only four-tick score in the set: free at runtime, black-box, architecture-agnostic, and the one entry tested on an embodiment it was not developed on. It ranks third only because it needs failed rollouts, and it inherits the trajectory-label noise FailureSpot documents. The humanoid test also caps it at 6 of 12 trials.
  • TDQC (#4) The best theory and the cleanest head-to-head, since it runs on SAFE's own features and rollouts over 21 seeds. Same tier as ActProbe and SAFE, and it ranks between them: black-box like ActProbe, but it fails C4 outright at 53.69 ROC-AUC across environments, and its headline application needs a simulator at inference.
  • SAFE (#5) Defined the problem and still wins the one independent benchmark that scored the cheap alternatives against it. It loses its own tier to TDQC, which beat it on four of six benchmarks using its own released features and rollouts, and it is the only Tier 3 entry that also fails C2: the probe reads activations, so a closed policy is out of reach.
  • FailureSpot (#6) Identifies a real defect in every supervised detector above it and fixes it, worth 13.9 points of timestamp AUROC over SAFE. It is alone in Tier 4: a human has to watch each failed rollout and mark the step it began, which is the heaviest preparation anyone here asks for. Its evidence is also the thinnest, one benchmark with no real robot and no code, on a metric and an annotation set it authored.

The two contested cells

Are a policy's own action probabilities any use? SAFE says no, reporting 50.25 on OpenVLA+LIBERO, and TDQC says yes and names the earlier finding. They ran different experiments: SAFE tested static transforms of those probabilities, TDQC trains a recurrent head on them against the episode outcome, reaching 72.72 on unseen tasks, above SAFE's own hidden-state probe. Uncalibrated they carry nothing; calibrated against the terminal label they are enough to monitor a closed API.

Do chunk consistency and magnitude suffice? ActProbe builds its method on them; FailureSpot computes the same two signals and reports 30.7. Also different experiments: ActProbe trains them against outcome labels, FailureSpot uses them as a self-supervised pseudo-label with no outcomes at all. They are informative features and near-useless targets, which is what the two opposing headlines conceal.

Ranks are judgements about what each detector needs and what it reads, not a leaderboard: the accuracy numbers are not comparable across these papers.
